First Lady brokers a local ceasefire to evacuate a trapped Ukrainian town
items.summary:
The White House said Friday that First Lady Melania Trump has secured a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine for Oleshky, a Russian-controlled front-line city in southern Ukraine. The pause is set to begin October 29 and is intended to let humanitarian aid in and let civilians leave through a designated safe passage.

Oleshky, occupied since February 2022 and sitting on the left bank of the Dnipro in the Kherson region, still holds an estimated 1,700 to 2,000 residents, most of them elderly, plus a few dozen children. The first lady described limited electricity, mined roads and regular attacks, with urgent needs for medicine, food and clean water. Under the plan, non-military teams from both countries would visit residents at home, assess what help each person needs, and arrange transport for anyone who wants to leave — to Russia or to Ukraine, by their own choice — while an American media organization documents the process.

The deal fits a pattern in Melania Trump's public work on children displaced by the war, including efforts this year to return children taken to Russia. It also lands while President Donald Trump is pressing Kyiv and Moscow toward a broader settlement, after his envoy's recent meeting with Vladimir Putin set a high bar for wider talks — making this small, concrete agreement stand out against a stalled larger diplomacy.

Watch whether Moscow and Kyiv publicly confirm the terms, and whether the October 29 start holds. A successful evacuation would not end the war, but it would test whether narrowly scoped, civilian-focused deals can be negotiated and kept even when a comprehensive peace is not in reach.

items.title: Attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz hit a record high in October
items.summary:
October has become the worst month on record for attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, according to tracking by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. The institute counted 28 confirmed and reported attacks this month alone, and 113 since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in late February.

The scale of damage to oil shipping is striking. The International Maritime Organization lists more than 30 very large crude carriers damaged since the conflict began, including 11 in October — roughly 3.5 percent of the entire global supertanker fleet, with each ship able to carry about 2 million barrels. One week in early October saw a dozen ships attacked, the highest weekly total of the war. Analysts say more owners have been willing to load cargoes in the Gulf anyway, drawn by freight rates above $1 million a day and steep discounts on regional crude.

The pattern matters far beyond the strait. Researchers argue Iran is using the attacks to slow any recovery in shipments and keep pressure on global energy markets ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, when fuel prices are already a central voter concern. Maritime officials also warn the true toll is likely higher, because reporting by shippers is voluntary and incomplete.

Foreign ministers from European and Middle Eastern countries met in Istanbul on Friday with Hormuz at the top of the agenda, pushing for a diplomatic arrangement that restores full navigation rights. Watch whether that diplomacy produces any de-escalation, or whether November brings another record month.

items.title: Magnitude 7.0 earthquake kills at least 16 in remote northern Tibet
items.summary:
A magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck a remote, high-altitude part of northern Tibet late Thursday night, killing at least 16 people and injuring at least 54, according to official reports carried by the Associated Press. The U.S. Geological Survey placed the epicenter about 118 miles east-northeast of Nagqu, at a shallow depth of roughly 11 miles — the kind of shallow quake that shakes the surface harder.

Hundreds of homes collapsed around Nagqu, communications were knocked out in some areas, trains through the region were halted, and rockfalls closed a stretch of National Highway 317 to all but emergency vehicles. By Friday afternoon, local officials said search teams had completed three rounds of house-by-house checks, and more than 5,000 people from three counties had joined the response. Thousands of tents, prefabricated housing units, folding beds and winter supplies were rushed in.

The rescue is racing the weather as much as the rubble. The area is sparsely populated but bitterly cold, intermittent snow is expected over the next three days, and aftershocks — including a magnitude 5.2 within the first hour — are continuing. President Xi Jinping ordered an all-out rescue and medical effort Friday morning, a step he reserves for major disasters.

Tibet sits where the Indian and Eurasian plates collide, one of the most earthquake-prone zones on Earth. Watch for updated casualty counts as crews reach outlying villages, and for whether displaced families can be sheltered before the snow arrives.

items.title: Typhoon Champi kills one, injures dozens and shuts down travel across Taiwan
items.summary:
Typhoon Champi battered Taiwan on Friday with powerful winds, torrential rain and dangerous coastal waves. Taiwanese authorities reported one person dead — swept away by waves on Liuqiu, a small island southwest of the main island — and 94 people injured, with nearly 1,300 residents evacuated from mountainous areas as a precaution.

The storm effectively paused air travel for the island. Taiwan cancelled 262 domestic flights and 669 international flights for Friday, and officials warned of flooding and landslides in areas where heavy rain falls on steep terrain. Gusts were reported above 90 mph in Japan's southern islands as the storm approached.

Champi's path now points north. After passing northeastern Taiwan, it is forecast to turn toward China's eastern coast, including waters near Shanghai, and then southern Japan, where carriers including Japan Airlines and ANA cancelled more than 100 flights scheduled between Friday and Sunday. Okinawa and the Yaeyama islands are expected to take strong winds and heavy rain as it passes.

For Taiwan, the immediate questions are flood damage, power restoration and whether rains trigger landslides in evacuated mountain districts. For the wider region, watch the storm's strength as it nears the Chinese coast this weekend.

items.title: South Korea again proposes military talks with the North to pin down the border line
items.summary:
South Korea's defense ministry on Friday renewed its proposal for military talks with North Korea, aimed at agreeing on the exact location of the land border between the two countries and reducing the risk of an accidental clash. Deputy Minister for National Defense Policy Kim Hong-cheol announced the offer in Seoul.

The push follows a landmine explosion inside the Demilitarized Zone last month that seriously injured South Korean soldiers. Seoul's investigation concluded the mines had been buried south of the Military Demarcation Line by North Korea — a finding Pyongyang rejects. South Korean officials say Northern troops building tactical roads and fences and laying mines near the line in recent years have at times crossed it, and that the two sides genuinely disagree about where parts of the line run, in part because some markers from the 1953 armistice have been lost over time.

This is not the first unanswered offer. Seoul proposed similar talks last November to resolve the same dispute and received no response, and North Korea's leadership has recently hardened its posture, with Kim Yo Jong visiting front-line areas and threatening retaliation for any interference with the North's border fortification work.

The stakes are less about a grand bargain than about accident prevention: when both armies patrol a boundary they locate differently, a routine encounter can escalate. Watch for any reply from Pyongyang — even a rejection would clarify whether any military communication channel is functioning at all.

items.title: Austria expels four Russian diplomats over alleged spying
items.summary:
Austria's foreign ministry said Friday it is expelling four Vienna-based Russian diplomats, declaring them personae non gratae over activity it described as incompatible with their diplomatic status — the standard diplomatic phrasing for espionage. The ministry said the decision rested on findings by Austrian security authorities.

Three of the four worked at Russia's embassy to Austria. The fourth was attached to Russia's delegation to the OSCE, the European security organization headquartered in Vienna, where he worked on military security and arms control. Russia's embassy called the move another unfriendly step and promised a response.

The expulsions bring Austria's total since 2020 to 18 Russian diplomats. Austria is formally neutral and does not belong to NATO, but its governments have sided politically with Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. In a previous round in May, Vienna pointed to a dense array of antennas on Russian diplomatic rooftops as a spying concern.

Vienna hosts the OSCE, the International Atomic Energy Agency and other U.N. bodies, and its large diplomatic community has long made it a hub for intelligence work under diplomatic cover. Watch for a reciprocal expulsion of Austrian diplomats from Moscow, the usual next step in these exchanges.

## POLITICS (6 items)

items.title: Justice Department sues to block Alaska from certifying its Senate race if the Republican loses
items.summary:
The Justice Department has sued to stop Alaska from certifying its U.S. Senate election if Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan loses, arguing that a second candidate with a nearly identical name — retired schoolteacher Daniel J. Sullivan — could confuse voters. The department asked a federal court on October 22 to declare any result affected by that confusion unlawful and to hold up certification pending an investigation into whether votes for one Sullivan were meant for the other.

The race is genuinely close and genuinely consequential. Sullivan faces Democrat Mary Peltola, a former state representative, in a contest that could help decide Senate control, with Democrats needing a net gain of four seats. The other Sullivan is a registered Republican listed on the ballot without a party label, while the incumbent is marked as the Republican incumbent; Alaska's state Supreme Court already approved keeping the challenger's name on the November 3 ballot. In the primary, the incumbent drew about 68,700 votes to the other Sullivan's roughly 4,100.

Legal experts reacted with unusual bluntness. Notre Dame election law professor Derek Muller called the department's theory — built on language in federal voting law about protecting the integrity of elections — one of the weakest he has seen, and noted that Alaska's ranked-choice system actually blunts name confusion, since a voter can rank both Sullivans. CNN's reporting added that ballots are co-mingled, making the requested after-the-fact investigation of voter intent nearly impossible to carry out.

The case has been assigned to Judge Sharon Gleason, and the administration has not yet sought emergency action. Watch for Alaska's response and any ruling before Election Day — the suit tests how far the federal government can go in intervening in a state's election before a single general-election vote is counted.

items.title: Federal judge bars Homeland Security voter-fraud door-knocks in nine states through Election Day
items.summary:
A federal judge in California has barred the Department of Homeland Security from conducting election-related field operations and interviews involving people known or reasonably suspected to be U.S. citizens in nine states, through the close of polls on November 3. Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín of the Northern District of California issued the order Wednesday in a challenge to the administration's push to investigate suspected noncitizen voting.

The covered states are California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin. The judge found the plaintiffs — including nurses' organizations, San Francisco and Santa Clara counties, and the Voto Latino Foundation — were likely to succeed on their claim that the operation runs afoul of the Voting Rights Act's ban on intimidating voters and those who help them vote. Reporting on the order described target lists built from tens of millions of records of uneven quality, with reviewers given only minutes to clear a name.

The administration's stated goal is to prevent unlawful voting by noncitizens, which remains illegal and which the court did not say cannot be investigated at all. The ruling targets a narrower problem: sending agents to the doors of people who may well be citizens, based on error-prone matching, in the final days before an election.

Timing is the immediate story. The judge paused her own order until 5 p.m. Friday to give the government a chance to seek emergency relief from the 9th Circuit. Watch that deadline — whether the injunction takes effect tonight will shape what federal agents can do in nine states for the last 11 days of the campaign.

items.title: Voters tell pollsters the next Congress should focus on costs and ending the Iran war — not on Trump
items.summary:
A new AP-NORC poll finds that voters in both parties want the next Congress, whoever controls it, to concentrate on lowering the cost of living and ending the war with Iran. About 8 in 10 registered voters rank reducing living costs among the highest priorities, and roughly 7 in 10 say the same about ending the Iran conflict.

By comparison, only about 4 in 10 want investigating the Trump administration to be a top priority, and only about 2 in 10 want Congress to prioritize advancing President Donald Trump's agenda. Even among Republicans, support is tepid: only about 4 in 10 Republican voters call backing Trump's agenda a highest priority, putting it behind costs, the war and the deficit. The poll of 1,119 adults was conducted October 8–12 and carries a margin of error of plus or minus 3.9 points.

Beneath the broad agreement sit real splits. Democratic voters who identify as democratic socialists are far more likely to demand investigations of the administration and an end to military aid to Israel, while MAGA Republicans are far more likely to want Congress behind Trump's program. Moderates in both parties are the most inclined to want the two sides to find common ground.

For candidates in the final stretch, the message is practical rather than ideological: kitchen-table costs and an unpopular war are what voters say they will judge the next Congress on. Watch whether the party that wins in November actually sequences its first 100 days that way, or lets its loudest faction set the agenda instead.

items.title: Trump rallies in Fort Myers as Florida's early vote and a tight governor's race take shape
items.summary:
President Donald Trump headlined a midterm rally Friday afternoon at Florida Gulf Coast University's Alico Arena in Fort Myers, stumping for Florida Republicans less than two weeks before Election Day. Doors opened at 10:30 a.m. for the 4,633-seat arena, with Trump scheduled to speak at 2 p.m., Senator Rick Scott and gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds among the scheduled speakers, and temporary flight restrictions in place around Southwest Florida International Airport for his arrival.

Ahead of the rally, Trump posted a full Florida endorsement slate Thursday night — Ashley Moody for Senate, Donalds for governor, James Uthmeier for attorney general and Wilton Simpson for agriculture commissioner, plus House candidates including Greg Steube and Jim Schwartzel. Donalds, a Naples congressman, faces Democrat David Jolly in a governor's race that has tightened, with polling averages showing Donalds ahead by roughly five points.

Florida's early numbers add tension to the visit. As of Friday morning, Democrats had cast more than 800,000 ballots to Republicans' roughly 771,000, driven by a mail-ballot edge, while Republicans led in early in-person voting in counties that had opened — about 14 percent of the state's 13.7 million registered voters had already voted, with statewide early in-person voting starting Saturday.

Fort Myers is one stop on an aggressive closing barnstorm — Georgia on Saturday and Michigan on Sunday follow. Watch whether Trump's presence moves the governor's race, and whether Republicans erase the Democratic mail-ballot lead once in-person early voting opens statewide.

items.title: In Iowa, Trump asks red-state voters to pretend he is on the ballot
items.summary:
President Donald Trump rallied a crowd at Sioux Gateway Airport in Sioux City on Thursday, standing with Iowa's top Republican candidates and making an explicit ask of voters in a state he carried by 13 points in 2024: pretend he himself is on the ballot. He praised Senate candidate Ashley Hinson as a mother, a warrior and a patriot, and governor candidate Zach Lahn as a longtime supporter.

The visit itself is the tell. Iowa, normally safe Republican ground, has competitive races for governor, Senate and three House seats, and Trump has recently toured other states he won by wide margins — Oklahoma, Alabama, Tennessee and Kentucky among them. A New York Times/Siena poll of likely Iowa voters found only 40 percent approving of his job performance, with half saying his policies have hurt the state, as diesel prices driven up by the Iran war squeeze farm country.

Republicans are counting on the deep-red 4th District around Sioux City to run up margins large enough to carry statewide races, as it did in a close governor's race in 2018. The district holds more than half the party's statewide registration advantage. Notably absent from the stage were the two Republican House incumbents in the state's most competitive districts, both of whom recently broke with Trump to back a resolution curbing his war powers.

Hinson, who has distanced herself from the president on issues like foreign beef imports while opposing the war-powers resolution, warned the crowd Iowa could be the seat that decides Senate control. Trump returns to Dubuque on November 1. Watch turnout in western Iowa — if the firewall underperforms, several statewide races could flip at once.

items.title: Two former FBI officials charged Friday with lying to Congress about Hunter Biden probe
items.summary:
In a genuinely new midday development Friday, the Justice Department unsealed charges against two former senior FBI officials, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, each facing one count of making a false statement to Congress. The complaint accuses them of concealing their task force's engagement with the Hunter Biden investigations and impeding the congressional inquiry, based on testimony they gave to the House Judiciary Committee in 2023.

Prosecutors and FBI Director Kash Patel say Floris led the Foreign Influence Task Force as a deputy assistant director from mid-2019 to mid-2022 and Benavides was its section chief through the 2020 election, and that both testified the task force was not involved, while documents, communications and witnesses say otherwise. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro highlighted a claim that one of them told Congress he had learned of the laptop investigation from Wikipedia. Both defendants appeared in federal court in Washington Friday morning, will not be detained, and have a hearing scheduled Tuesday.

The judge's remarks are part of the story. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui noted the charge is rare, was brought by complaint rather than a grand jury indictment, and told prosecutors to be ready to move forward given the seriousness of charging two decorated agents over events from years ago. Floris's lawyers called the case baseless, said it rests on the say-so of politicians, and pointed to the timing less than two weeks before Election Day.

The charges do not themselves prove the underlying claims about how the bureau handled the Biden investigations — a special counsel's earlier probe resulted in tax and gun charges against Hunter Biden, who was later pardoned, and a separate informant was charged with making false bribery claims. Watch Tuesday's hearing for the specific statements prosecutors intend to prove false.

items.title: SpaceX wants 80,000 cell sites to become a fourth national phone carrier
items.summary:
SpaceX is reportedly in talks to secure access to at least 80,000 cell sites across the United States, a scale that would lay the groundwork for a fourth nationwide wireless network alongside AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile. The report, citing people familiar with the discussions, sent the three incumbent carriers down roughly 4 to 5 percent in extended trading, while SpaceX shares rose about 1.4 percent after hours.

Tower owners moved the other way. Crown Castle, named as one of the infrastructure firms approached, jumped about 9 percent, and American Tower added about 5 percent, because a new national tenant would mean large, long-term lease deals potentially worth billions. SpaceX has already bought low-band spectrum and has federal approval for 15,000 satellites designed to connect directly to phones, and Elon Musk said on this week's earnings call that building the ground network is how Starlink Mobile becomes a major U.S. carrier.

The stakes are about structure, not just one stock move. U.S. mobile service has been a three-player market for years, and a well-funded fourth entrant with its own spectrum and satellite layer would pressure prices and coverage claims. The counterweight is cost and time: analysts cited in follow-on coverage put a nationwide ground build at more than $80 billion and years of work.

Watch whether any tower company confirms a lease agreement, and whether regulators attach conditions to SpaceX's spectrum and satellite plans as the ground and space pieces come together.

items.title: Big Tech earnings and the Fed will test a shaky AI rally next week
items.summary:
Investors head into the busiest week of earnings season with the AI trade on the defensive. Thursday's selloff — the Nasdaq's biggest one-day drop since June, with the semiconductor index down sharply — followed disappointing reactions to results from Meta and Lam Research, and it has raised the bar for what comes next.

Alphabet and Microsoft report on Wednesday and Amazon on Thursday, in a week when roughly a third of the S&P 500 posts results. Third-quarter earnings for the index are so far tracking up more than 32 percent from a year ago, and strategists quoted by Reuters say strong numbers from the big spenders are what would turn the pullback into a buying opportunity rather than the start of a deeper correction. The focus will be less on headline profit than on guidance for capital spending, expected at around $800 billion this year for the hyperscalers, and on any evidence of returns on that outlay.

The Federal Reserve meets the same Wednesday. Futures late Thursday put only about a 5 percent chance on another rate hike at that meeting — the Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023 — but put roughly an 80 percent chance on a hike in December, so Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference language matters as much as the decision itself.

Watch the capex guidance first, then Warsh's hints on December. Chip results from Intel and SanDisk, plus Eli Lilly, Exxon, Chevron and Caterpillar, will broaden the read on whether weakness stays narrowly in AI names.

items.title: Data-center backlash is starting to break projects, not just slow them
items.summary:
Australia's NextDC became the clearest example yet this week of local opposition hitting a data-center operator's finances. Its shares closed down 42 percent on October 21 after it cut its underlying earnings forecast for the year to June by more than a third, to A$245 million to A$265 million, paused every project not already backed by a customer contract, launched a detailed review of its capital spending, and said it may sell development sites it no longer needs soon.

The trigger was power, not demand for computing. Utility Jemena suspended work to boost supply to NextDC's M3 site in Melbourne after community opposition, following an episode last month in which residents used vehicles and other means to block installation of tall concrete poles for 66,000-volt lines the site requires. The company still cited about A$8.7 billion of liquidity at the end of September, which underlines that this was a delivery and permission problem, not a cash crisis.

The same pattern appeared in the U.S. this week. On October 20 Amazon abandoned plans for four data centers on a Virginia site it had bought from George Washington University after local opposition, and agreed to donate $5 million to the county housing trust fund.

For the AI buildout, this reframes the bottleneck. Chips and money have dominated the story; grid connections, poles, and neighborhood consent are now visibly capable of stranding planned capacity. Watch for other operators to distinguish more sharply between contracted, powered sites and speculative land banks.

items.title: Western Digital beats on AI storage demand — and still gets sold
items.source: Morningstar / Dow Jones Newswires (Wall Street Journal reporter)
items.summary:
Western Digital reported fiscal first-quarter profit of $1.78 billion, or $4.63 a share, up from $1.15 billion a year earlier, with adjusted earnings of $4.64 a share against analyst expectations around $4.11. Revenue rose to $4.38 billion from $2.82 billion a year ago, also ahead of the roughly $4.14 billion expected, driven by demand for hard drives used in computers and AI data centers and by improved pricing.

Management guided the current quarter well above the prior-year pace, to adjusted earnings of $5.60 to $6.00 a share on revenue of $5 billion to $5.2 billion, and raised the quarterly dividend 17 percent to 17.5 cents a share, payable December 17 to holders of record December 4. Its finance chief credited continued momentum, strong growth in total capacity shipped, and better pricing.

The market reaction is the second half of the story. Follow-on coverage noted the shares erased an early after-hours gain and fell in line with the broader AI selloff on Thursday, despite the beat and raise. That disconnect is a useful midday signal: on a day when investors are questioning AI spending, even a supplier posting 55 percent revenue growth is being traded as part of the group first and on its own numbers second.

Watch whether the stock separates from the chip-led move next week when the hyperscalers report, since their spending plans are the demand source behind storage orders like these.

items.title: Hoka and UGG maker says rivals' discounting is hurting premium shoes
items.summary:
Deckers Outdoor, the company behind UGG boots and Hoka running shoes, reported second-quarter sales of $1.48 billion, just below the $1.51 billion analysts expected, even as profit rose 27 percent for the quarter ended September 30. Its shares fell about 8 percent in extended trading, and follow-on Friday coverage showed the stock down again in the morning session as it also cut its full-year sales outlook to roughly $5.70 billion to $5.73 billion.

Chief executive Stefano Caroti told analysts that promotional activity in the U.S. increased through the quarter, especially in athletic footwear, and weighed on the company's online sales because Deckers held to full-price discipline. Comparable direct-to-consumer sales fell 6.4 percent. He said the company is most exposed below $120, where competition is densest, and that it will keep prioritizing margin and long-term brand value over chasing near-term sales that would dilute the brands.

Analysts quoted by Reuters said the pressure was not limited to lower-income shoppers. Share losses showed up across income brackets, including higher-income consumers, as buyers became more selective — a warning sign for premium brands that have relied on affluent customers holding up.

This matters beyond one footwear name because it tests a broader consumer claim: that premium products are insulated. If discounting by larger rivals like Nike is pulling even well-off shoppers toward deals, other premium consumer brands reporting this season face the same question.

items.title: American Express posts record quarter, beats on earnings, trims nothing on spending
items.summary:
American Express reported third-quarter earnings of $4.68 a share on Friday, beating the consensus estimate of $4.47 and rising from $4.14 a year earlier. Revenue was $20.06 billion for the quarter ended in September, up 8.9 percent from $18.43 billion a year ago and just 0.34 percent below consensus — a near-match that other Friday coverage described as record revenue, with net income up 28 percent to $3.7 billion on a reported basis.

Detail in the Friday reporting pointed to billed business up about 8 percent, U.S. consumer spending up 9.4 percent, travel and entertainment spending up 10 percent, card-fee growth accelerating to 17 percent, and about 3.1 million new cards acquired, with credit quality described as stable. The company raised reported full-year earnings guidance in its filing, while also disclosing efficiency actions including a workforce reduction of roughly 5 percent in some coverage of the release.

The contrast with the footwear and AI names is instructive. Where Deckers described a more selective, promotion-hunting shopper, Amex's premium card base is still spending, especially on travel and experiences, and paying higher fees to do so. That split — premium services holding, premium goods discount-pressured — is a cleaner midday read on the consumer than either story alone.

Watch the updated full-year guidance and any call commentary on whether the Platinum refresh costs ease in the fourth quarter, which management flagged as a path to better operating leverage.

items.title: Pentagon lets DHS test a military heat ray for possible use at the southern border
items.summary:
The Pentagon has authorized the Department of Homeland Security to borrow and test the Active Denial System, a military device that fires an invisible beam of electromagnetic energy a little more than half a mile, according to a memo signed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last month and obtained by CNN. The beam produces an intense heating sensation on skin — officials have compared it to opening a hot oven — and an urge to move away, with a tingling effect described as lasting 10 to 15 minutes.

The memo covers a temporary loan of one system for seven months starting in September, says it is not to be operated by Defense personnel, and makes DHS solely responsible for employment, tactics and procedures. DHS can request further use afterward based on need. Customs and Border Protection told CNN it continually evaluates new technologies to strengthen mission capability, and the request as reported did not specify where or how testing would occur.

Using the system at the border would be unprecedented. It was briefly sent to Afghanistan nearly two decades ago but never used in combat, and officials considered and rejected border or crowd-control uses in earlier administrations, including in 2018 and during domestic unrest in 2020. Former officials quoted by CNN raised legal, use-of-force, sovereignty and safety questions — including the risk of people fleeing toward a river — and some agents questioned the need amid low crossings and increased staffing.

No deployment has been announced; this is permission to test and develop tactics. Watch for any DHS description of a test site, rules of use, or medical/legal review, which will determine whether this stays an experiment or becomes policy.

items.title: Federal government again stops sharing evidence in the Minnesota ICE shooting investigations
items.summary:
Minnesota officials say the federal government has again stopped sharing evidence with state investigators looking into the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal immigration officers during the administration's immigration crackdown in Minneapolis earlier this year. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said prosecutors were told on Sept. 10 that sharing would pause indefinitely, citing challenges with Washington.

The state sued the administration in March for access to materials it says it needs for an independent investigation. Prosecutors announced in July that the federal government had begun turning over evidence, including body-camera video and hard drives containing statements, and said they expected to receive everything. Recent October court filings say that transfer stopped soon after it began.

What the state says it still does not have is central to the cases: the cellphones of the officers involved, recordings of key interviews including a statement by one officer who shot Pretti, the firearms used, and physical evidence such as projectiles and shell casings. The administration has suggested state prosecutors lack jurisdiction to investigate federal officers, while Minnesota officials say they do not trust the federal government to investigate itself.

State prosecutors have asked a judge to order federal agencies to hand over the evidence, arguing there is no legal authority or rational basis for obstructing state criminal investigations. Watch for the judge's ruling on that renewed request.

items.title: Supreme Court lets New Hampshire bar student IDs at the polls for the midterms
items.summary:
The Supreme Court said Thursday that New Hampshire can fully enforce its ban on voters using student IDs as identification at the polls next month, handing Republicans a win in a fight over tightening voting procedures. The court paused a lower judge's ruling that poll workers could still consider a student ID case by case when a voter lacks an approved government-issued ID.

New Hampshire's legislature removed student IDs from the expressly valid forms of identification, and the secretary of state went further, directing officials not to consider them even as backup evidence. A federal judge declined to block the law itself but blocked that broader directive on Oct. 2. Secretary of State David Scanlan asked the Supreme Court to intervene, arguing the order injected uncertainty less than three weeks before the election.

The challengers, the Coalition for Open Democracy, argue the change discriminates against younger voters and note the state offered no security concern specific to student IDs. The justices' action rests on the principle that courts should not alter election rules on the eve of an election, not on a final ruling that the law is constitutional.

The stakes are heightened because New Hampshire's U.S. Senate race is among those that will decide Senate control. Students voting in the state should check the secretary of state's current ID guidance and bring an accepted government document.

items.title: Hegseth's staff damaged a historic Eisenhower globe moving it for his office
items.summary:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's staff damaged a standing globe believed to have been used by Gen. Dwight D. Eisenhower during World War II while trying to move it into Hegseth's Pentagon office, the Washington Post first reported and the Pentagon acknowledged on Oct. 22. The Army confirmed the damage happened Feb. 3 during an attempted move.

The 30-inch globe, dating to the 1930s, was dropped, leaving damage to its shell near Antarctica and detaching it from the metal mount that lets it rotate. It never reached Hegseth's office. Normally trained curators from the U.S. Army Center of Military History would handle such a move, but those staff were furloughed during a partial government shutdown, and Hegseth's staff attempted it themselves.

The Pentagon's statement was brief: accidents happen, no one was harmed, and the globe is being repaired. The department did not provide a repair cost or timeline. Two Eisenhower globes are housed at the Pentagon and are considered priceless artifacts from his service as supreme Allied commander, before he became the 34th president.

The story is a small one with a clear lesson about process: an irreplaceable artifact survived a world war, then was cracked during an office move made without the specialists assigned to protect it.

items.title: Federal plan aims to catch kidney disease earlier and open up dialysis and transplant care
items.source: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
items.summary:
The Department of Health and Human Services launched a Kidney Care National Plan on Oct. 20, a department-wide strategy to detect kidney disease earlier, expand treatment and home-care options, and strengthen safety and competition across dialysis and transplantation. Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced the plan in Fort Worth as part of the administration's chronic-disease agenda.

The scale explains the push. HHS estimates about 37 million American adults have kidney disease, and most do not know it, so treatment often begins only after significant damage has occurred. About 558,000 Americans receive dialysis, roughly 90,000 are on the kidney transplant waiting list, and two large chains control about 74 percent of the dialysis market, up from about 59 percent in 2006.

The plan targets what HHS calls structural problems: certification and regulatory barriers that discourage new dialysis providers, payment incentives that reward late-stage treatment over prevention, and an organ-procurement system it says needs stronger oversight, including decertification of poor performers and a shift toward a multi-vendor transplant network.

The plan sets priorities rather than changing care rules immediately. Watch for the specific steps that follow — a possible early-diagnosis payment model, streamlined certification for new providers, and how dialysis incumbents and transplant organizations respond.

items.title: Severe storms with large hail target New Mexico and Colorado as Hurricane Vance strengthens offshore
items.summary:
The main U.S. weather concern on Friday is the Southwest and nearby High Plains, where severe thunderstorms are expected across parts of New Mexico and southern Colorado into tonight. Forecasters say hail is the primary hazard, with isolated strong wind gusts and a tornado or two also possible, following two days of storms that hit Arizona.

The same system brings a flash-flood risk. The Weather Prediction Center kept a slight risk of excessive rainfall over the broader region, warning that repeated storms over ground already soaked by Thursday rain — especially from the Jemez and San Juan Mountains toward Mount Taylor — could produce rapid runoff and localized flooding, separate from ongoing river flooding in northwest New Mexico.

Offshore, Hurricane Vance in the eastern Pacific was forecast to keep strengthening and become a major hurricane by tonight, tracking north-northwest off Mexico's coast with no watches or warnings in effect Friday morning. In southern Florida, heavy showers and thunderstorms are expected to increase this weekend, with localized flash flooding possible in low-lying and urban areas.

For anyone in the storm zone, the practical steps are the familiar ones: follow National Weather Service warnings, avoid flooded roads, and treat large hail as a reason to get vehicles under cover early rather than after storms fire.

items.title: Guardians manager Stephen Vogt says he is staying in Cleveland
items.summary:
Cleveland Guardians manager Stephen Vogt put an end to speculation about a move to Seattle, telling reporters on Thursday that he will be back in Cleveland next season. He said he has not received a call from the Mariners and described the talk about a departure as media-driven.

The rumors had a plausible backstory. Vogt worked as Seattle's bullpen coach in 2023 before Cleveland hired him, and his family home is in Olympia, Washington. Seattle's job came open after the club fired Dan Wilson last month following a 76-86 season. Vogt, 41, has won a division title in each of his three seasons in Cleveland and has twice been named American League Manager of the Year.

For Cleveland, keeping Vogt preserves continuity for one of baseball's youngest rosters just days after an AL Championship Series loss to Tampa Bay extended the franchise's World Series drought to 76 years. Team president Chris Antonetti said he expects Vogt to manage in Cleveland for a long time and that the club has no interest in letting him manage elsewhere, though a rare manager trade remains theoretically possible if Seattle calls.

Pitching coach Carl Willis will also return for another season, and Vogt used the same session to explain that starter Tanner Bibee's limited postseason use was a matchup decision favoring left-handed pitching — a conversation he said he had directly with an upset Bibee before Game 6 of the ALCS.

items.title: State offers cash as a 'final' try to settle Clintonville ravine bridge fight
items.summary:
Ohio has offered $42,000 in cash as what it calls a final attempt to win approval for a bridge through Bill Moose Run, a protected ravine in Columbus's Clintonville neighborhood. The letter, obtained by The Dispatch on Oct. 22, asks the Franklin Soil and Water Conservation District to sign off on the project, with a response requested by Oct. 30.

The 73-acre tract north of Morse Road, between North High Street and Indianola Avenue, has been covered by a perpetual conservation easement since 1999. The state owns the land but the conservation district controls the easement. The Ohio schools for the blind and for the deaf, on opposite sides of the ravine, want a two-lane road and pedestrian path roughly 46 to 59 feet wide connecting their campuses, arguing it is needed for student safety and accessibility, and about $13.6 million in state funding has already been appropriated.

The two sides have traded and rejected mitigation offers for months. The conservation district sought 13.2 acres of additional protected land; the state countered with 6 acres of scattered, noncontiguous land. In an Oct. 19 letter the district said it would not approve the bridge without either the full 13.2 acres or a less damaging design, citing forest canopy, water quality and wildlife habitat. Three days later the state rejected that and offered the cash instead, calling it a fair value for the 2 acres needed for the bridge.

Neighbors have opposed the project over environmental harm, the precedent of overriding a perpetual easement, and a lack of transparency after work was seen on the site in fall 2025. What to watch: the conservation district's next board meeting is Nov. 9, after the state's Oct. 30 response deadline.

items.title: Ohio State faculty warn Chase Center puts academic freedom at risk
items.summary:
A faculty committee at Ohio State University told the University Senate on Oct. 22 that the Salmon P. Chase Center for Civics, Culture & Society poses a credible threat to academic freedom. The report from the Committee on Academic Freedom and Responsibility focused on the power the center's director holds over curriculum and on what it called the center's ideological mission.

The Chase Center was not created through normal university channels. A 2023 state law, Senate Bill 117, mandated five such independent centers at Ohio public universities, with Ohio State's housed in the John Glenn College of Public Affairs and authorized to hire 15 tenure-track faculty. Philosophy professor Tristram McPherson, presenting the report, said the law gives the director complete curricular oversight — effectively the power to decide unilaterally what is and is not taught — and stressed the concern is about the structure, not current director Lee Strang personally.

Faculty at the center pushed back in the same meeting. Professor Michael Clune said Chase Center faculty have never felt their academic freedom diminished, that the director is accountable to the provost, president and trustees, and that the committee never spoke with center faculty before issuing its findings. An undergraduate senator raised the same objection, warning the effort could become a political gesture rather than real reform.

The stakes extend beyond one center. A pending Statehouse bill, Senate Bill 461, introduced in June, would lock in funding and independence for all five centers, give directors sole authority over hiring, promotion, tenure and curriculum, and elevate the Ohio State and Toledo directors to deans by Jan. 1. Senators voted to take the report up further in steering committee with center members involved.

items.title: Ohio puts $1 million behind domestic-violence shelters and police training
items.summary:
Ohio is creating new grant programs for domestic-violence shelters and law enforcement agencies, Gov. Mike DeWine announced Thursday. The centerpiece is $1 million for the state's 55 recognized domestic-violence shelters, structured as a one-time $18,000 grant to each shelter for emergency services and support for victims and their dependents.

The announcement was backed by a sobering state analysis. Reviewing 2 million arrests, the Ohio Department of Public Safety's Office of Criminal Justice Services found that more than half of Ohio's violent-crime arrests from 1974 to 2023 involved domestic violence — and that share has not improved over time.

Alongside the shelter money, the state will fund ballistic shields for officers answering high-risk calls, training in lethality assessments that help officers identify survivors at highest risk and connect them to crisis help and safety planning, and co-responder grants that pair victim advocates with law enforcement on domestic-violence calls. DeWine also directed a state police advisory board to develop a statewide standard for domestic-violence response and investigation, drawing on an April handbook from the Ohio Domestic Violence Network, which will run seven free regional training sessions for officers.

For local shelters and departments, including those in Northeast Ohio, the practical question is timing — when applications open and how quickly the one-time money reaches programs that operate on thin margins.

items.title: Springfield Haitian residents are mid-march on a 40-mile walk to the Statehouse
items.summary:
Members of Springfield's Haitian community are in the middle of a four-day, more than 40-mile march from Springfield to the Ohio Statehouse in Columbus, running Oct. 21-24. By midday Friday they are on the road for a third day, headed toward a closing rally at 1 p.m. Oct. 24 at West Bank Park in Columbus.

The march follows the end of temporary protected status for Haitians. An estimated 15,000 Haitians were living in Springfield under TPS when the U.S. Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to end it in June. Residents were ordered to report to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement office outside Cincinnati, and some were fitted with ankle monitors — a practice that drew national attention after the family of 20-year-old Pierre Damas Bel said shame and bullying over his monitor drove him to die by stepping under a moving truck.

The marchers are asking the government to end ankle monitoring, remove ICE agents from Springfield, return detained Haitians to their families, and establish permanent protected status for Haitians in the United States. Pastor Gilbert Joubert Adrien, who was detained by ICE in August and released on bond Sept. 15, led a community worship in Springfield on the march's first night.

What to watch: whether state or federal officials respond when the march reaches Columbus on Saturday, and whether the rally draws counter-demonstrations or official meetings.

items.title: Peak fall color and a dry, sunny weekend settle over Northeast Ohio
items.summary:
Greater Akron and Northeast Ohio are heading into a stretch of sunny days with no rain expected at least through Thursday, according to the National Weather Service. Friday and Saturday are forecast sunny with highs near 66, Sunday climbs to near 69, and Monday could reach 71.

The timing lines up with fall color. The Ohio Department of Natural Resources says leaves have changed nearly everywhere, with hickories turning bright yellow and sweet gums showing red and purple. ODNR Fall Color Forester David Parrott said reporters across the state are seeing mostly near-peak and peak conditions, calling it a great time to get outdoors this weekend.

The trade-off is cold nights. Lows are expected in the 30s, around 37 on Friday and Saturday nights, with a chance of frost in some areas Sunday night into Monday morning — worth noting for anyone with sensitive plants still outside or outdoor plumbing to protect.

For local families, it is a clean window for fall outings — trails, orchards and the zoo weekend — before any rain chance returns later next week.

baby.tip: Paperwork and go-bag week: do one final hospital-bag check together — IDs and insurance cards, phone chargers, snacks and a change of clothes for Mike, and a going-home outfit for the baby in two sizes, since newborn and 0-3 month fits vary a lot. Put the bag by the door and the car seat base check on the same list, and if anything about pre-registration or where to check in is unclear, ask your OB's office this week while it's still a calm question.
baby.fact: Newborns arrive already knowing the sounds of home. Babies can recognize their mother's voice at birth from hearing it in the womb, and they are calmed by familiar voices and rhythms — which is why talking, humming, and reading to the baby now, and in those first days, genuinely registers.
baby.fun: Tiny mission for today: start the family birth pool, just for fun. Mike, Kelly, and the grandparents each write down a predicted date, time, and weight, seal them in an envelope, and open it together after the baby arrives. Closest guess picks the first celebratory takeout order.
